title: Transport in multilayer graphene: resistance from stacking faults
authors: C. M. Wilson, R. Ganesh, K. V. Samokhin
abstract: arXiv:2610.20713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multilayer graphene exhibits rich possibilities for stacking. While natural bulk graphite predominantly occurs in the Bernal structure, where layers are stacked in an $-ABAB-$ pattern, rhombohedral stacking has sprung to prominence recently. It is well known that Bernal graphite exhibits anisotropic transport, with high resistance to currents along the stacking axis. Careful experiments using pillar geometries have measured out-of-plane resistance, attributing it to stacking faults where planes slip out of the nominal $ABAB$ sequence. The observed resistance shows anomalously large, non-Gaussian, sample-to-sample variations. In this article, we build a theoretical framework to calculate $c$-axis resistance of graphene stacks with an arbitrary stacking arrangement. Our approach builds on the idea that, regardless of stacking sequence, we have in-plane translational symmetry. With in-plane momentum as a good quantum number, $c$-axis transport reduces to an effectively one-dimensional problem that can be addressed using the Landauer paradigm. We calculate the resistances of a variety of simple stacking faults in both Bernal and rhombohedral systems. We also calculate the resistance of a rhombohedral 'slab' embedded between Bernal leads. Remarkably, despite both Bernal and rhombohedral graphite being metallic, the system exhibits insulating behaviour. We attribute this to Fermi surface mismatch. We next calculate the resistance of a multilayer sample with stacking disorder. Resistance is non-self-averaging, akin to a one-dimensional wire where disorder has a strong localizing effect. The median resistance grows exponentially with stack size, indicating insulating character driven by localization. Our results demonstrate that transport measurements on mesoscopic graphitic pillars serve as signatures of stacking faults, and in particular, probe localization-driven physics.
summary:
- Landauer‑based 1D model for c‑axis transport in multilayer graphene with arbitrary stacking.
- Calculated fault resistances show large, non‑Gaussian sample‑to‑sample variations due to Fermi‑surface mismatch.
- Rhombohedral slab embedded in Bernal leads behaves insulating, despite both phases being metallic.

title: All-temperature superfluidity in two dimensions
authors: Bilal Hawashin, Soumyadeep Chaudhuri, Igor F. Herbut, Michael M. Scherer
abstract: arXiv:2610.20717v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In local theories with short-range interactions, continuous symmetries cannot be spontaneously broken in two spatial dimensions at nonzero temperature. $\mathrm{U}(1)$-symmetric models instead admit a Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless (BKT) phase with quasi-long-range order and nonzero phase stiffness, which is normally destroyed at high temperatures by vortex proliferation. Here, we show that a BKT phase, and with it superfluidity, can persist to arbitrarily high temperatures. Using the large-$N$ expansion, we study a $(2+1)$-dimensional quantum field theory in which a complex scalar is coupled to the critical $\mathrm{O}(N)$ model. At the biconical fixed point, where the inter-sector coupling is negative, the thermal effective potential has a circle of minima with nonzero $\mathrm{U}(1)$ amplitude. Integrating out the gapped fluctuations yields an effective theory for the compact phase mode at distances large compared to $1/T$. Since temperature is the only scale at the fixed point, the phase stiffness grows linearly with temperature, with a proportionality factor that scales linearly with $N$ and is fixed entirely by the fixed point. This renders vortex operators irrelevant for sufficiently large $N$. We further show that the vortex fugacity is exponentially small in $N$.
summary:
- BKT superfluidity survives to arbitrarily high temperatures in a (2+‑D theory where a complex scalar couples to a critical O(N) model.
- At the biconical fixed point the phase stiffness scales linearly with temperature and with N, rendering vortex operators irrelevant for large N.
- Vortex fugacity is exponentially suppressed in N, ensuring stability of the high‑temperature superfluid phase.

title: Boundary-induced geometrical frustration in a square Rydberg-atom lattice
authors: Marco Rigobello, Luka Pave\v{s}i\'{c}, Daniel Jaschke, Pietro Silvi, Marco Di Liberto, Simone Montangero, Simone Notarnicola
abstract: arXiv:2610.20723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study geometric defects in square-lattice Rydberg-atom arrays induced by lattice-size parity in the striated density-wave phase. While odd-sized lattices select a single striated domain, even-sized lattices seed incompatible domains at the four corners, resulting in a {\pi}/2-rotation invariant state with a geometrical defect emanating from the lattice center. At larger detunings, we instead identify a {\pi}-rotation-invariant state with two domains nucleated by opposite corners and separated by a one-dimensional diagonal defect. We probe the state-preparation protocol on the Aquila atomic quantum processor and benchmark it with equilibrium and real-time dynamics tensor-network simulations. Our results assess the role of boundaries and lattice size in determining the global ordering in programmable quantum matter.
summary:
- Odd‑size lattices select a single striated domain; even‑size lattices seed incompatible corner domains, yielding a π/2‑rotation invariant state with a central defect.
- At larger detunings a π‑rotation invariant state appears, featuring two opposite‑corner domains separated by a diagonal defect.
- Experiments on Aquila and tensor‑network simulations confirm that boundaries and lattice size dictate global ordering in programmable quantum matter.

title: Long-lived local coherences at high temperature from frozen domain walls
abstract: arXiv:2610.20724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local coherences between distinct charge sectors--measured by the single-particle Green's function or the transverse spin autocorrelation function--do not overlap with hydrodynamic modes. At finite temperature, therefore, they decay faster than any power law in generic chaotic systems. We present a mechanism by which these coherences can persist anomalously long, for integrable and chaotic spin chains (including the XXZ and Fredkin spin chains) that obey a quantum group symmetry. We show--using a Mazur bound derived from the quantum-group symmetry, together with locality and a "non-undershoot" assumption--that the transverse spin autocorrelation function $C(t) \equiv \langle \sigma^-_x(t) \sigma^+_x(0)\rangle$ can decay at most algebraically: $C(t) \gtrsim 1/t^2$. This bound is not tight: in the large-anisotropy limit of the XXZ spin chain, at infinite temperature, we explicitly compute $C(t) \sim \sqrt{3}/(18 \sqrt{t})$. We also compute this decay rate in the XXZ spin chain for general easy-axis anisotropy, and estimate it to scale as $C(t) \sim t^{-2/z}$ (for transport exponent $z$) in the chaotic models.
summary:
- Shows that local coherences in spin chains with quantum‑group symmetry decay only algebraically, not faster than any power law.
- Derives a Mazur bound $C(t)\gtrsim1/t^2$ and computes explicit decay $C(t)\sim1/\sqrt{t}$ (large anisotropy) and $C(t)\sim t^{-2/z}$ (general anisotropy).
- Demonstrates that frozen domain walls in integrable and chaotic models (XXZ, Fredkin) protect long‑lived coherences even at high temperature.

title: Quantum oscillations in a solvable model of a Kondo insulator
authors: Abhisek Samanta, Mohit Randeria, Sumilan Banerjee
abstract: arXiv:2610.20734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the effects of interactions on the low-energy density of states (SdH) and magnetization (dHvA) quantum oscillations (QOs) in a Kondo insulator. Toward this end we introduce a generalization of the periodic Anderson model with Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) interactions at each site that is exactly solvable in the large-$N$ limit, where $N$ is the number of flavors of the heavy $f$ electrons. We show analytically and numerically that the insulating state remains stable in terms of spectrum, thermodynamics, and transport at low temperatures even for interaction strengths much larger than non-interacting band gap of the hybridization-gap insulator. We analytically derive generalizations of Lifshitz-Kosevich (LK) formulae, distinct for the SdH and dHvA QOs, for the interacting insulator. We find that the SdH oscillation frequencies, $F_0\pm \delta F$, corresponding to the conduction and valence band edges, can be weakly renormalized by interaction relative to their non-interacting values. In contrast, dHvA QO frequency $F_0$ is not renormalized by interactions, and remains the same as that for the non-interacting unhybridized bands. The QO amplitudes show a remarkable difference: the dHvA amplitude is essentially unaffected by interactions, while the SdH amplitude is strongly enhanced due to gap renormalization.
summary:
- Introduced solvable SYK‑enhanced periodic Anderson model; insulating state remains robust under strong interactions.
- Derived interacting Lifshitz‑Kosevich formulas: SdH frequencies shift slightly, dHvA frequency unchanged.
- SdH amplitude strongly enhanced by gap renormalization; dHvA amplitude largely unaffected.

title: Resonant enhancement of Raman scattering in a MoS$_2$ nanotube
authors: D. R. Kazanov, A. V. Poshakinskiy
abstract: arXiv:2610.20755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The whispering-gallery modes confined in the wall of a multiwall MoS$_2$ nanotube resonantly enhance the spontaneous Raman scattering by its own optical phonons. The enhancement is doubly resonant --- pump and Stokes waves hit two adjacent modes at one pump energy, and the signal scales as $(Q_{\rm pump}Q_{\rm sc})^2$ - whenever a phonon energy matches the free spectral range of the mode ladder. Near the A exciton the excitonic dispersion compresses the ladder and sweeps its spacing through all intralayer phonon energies of MoS$_2$, so the match, reached for $A_{1g}$ at $E_{\rm pump}=1551$~meV, requires no geometric tuning. A missed match splits the excitation peak into a pump- and a scattered-resonant doublet whose splitting measures the residual detuning. Selection rules confine the double resonance to the TM$\to$TM channel and exclude $E_{1g}$.
summary:
- Whispering‑gallery modes in a MoS₂ nanotube wall doubly resonantly enhance Raman scattering, scaling as \((Q_{\rm pump}Q_{\rm sc})^2\).
- Excitonic dispersion near the A exciton compresses the mode ladder, allowing a phonon‑energy match (A₁g at 1551 meV) without geometric tuning.
- A detuned resonance splits the peak into a pump‑ and scattered‑resonant doublet, confined to the TM→TM channel and excluding E₁g.

title: Enabling large language model agents for high-fidelity many-body perturbation theory calculations
authors: Benran Zhang, Byeongchan Lee, Zien Zhu, Chih-En Hsu, Zhenfa Zheng, Hung-Chung Hsueh, Young Woo Choi, Mauro Del Ben, Zhenglu Li
abstract: arXiv:2610.20779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) methods, including the GW approximation, the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) method, and GW perturbation theory (GWPT), among others, provide accurate first-principles descriptions of excited-state properties and multiparticle interactions of materials. However, their use remains limited due to complex multi-software workflows, interdependent physical parameters, and substantial theoretical expertise. Large language model (LLM) agents, which couple a language model to software tools, show potential in automating computational tasks, but MBPT remains an unaddressed challenge. We show that LLM agents tested in our work, including frontier models such as Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, do not reliably construct MBPT workflows in one attempt, suggesting that correct setup requires expert knowledge and consistency that current models lack. Across tested model-harness combinations, out-of-the-box agents average 54%, 36%, and 19% on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow benchmarks, with strong model dependence and large run-to-run variation. Errors typically originate from cross-stage inconsistencies that surface only several stages after they are introduced. We therefore develop AI-Donkey, an agentic framework that combines expert-curated knowledge with deterministic execution to enable high-fidelity GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT calculations and analyses. With AI-Donkey, all tested agents, from frontier proprietary models to open-weight models, produce complete, runnable MBPT workflows with no observed run-to-run variation. We further demonstrate autonomous calculations and post-processing on 1D, 2D, and bulk materials, including the many-body enhancement of Fr\"ohlich electron-phonon coupling in polar semiconductors. Our approach provides a general framework for knowledge engineering to enable reliable agentic workflows in computational materials science.
summary:
- LLM agents (Opus 7, GPT‑fail to reliably build MBPT workflows, achieving only 54 %, 36 %, and 19 % success on GW, GW‑BSE, and GWPT benchmarks.
- Errors stem from cross‑stage inconsistencies that appear only after several workflow steps, highlighting the need for expert knowledge and consistency.
- The AI‑Donkey framework merges curated expert rules with deterministic execution, enabling accurate GW, GW‑BSE, and GWPT calculations across tested agents.

title: Modeling Transport and Mechanics in Anion Exchange Membranes to Optimize Continuous CO2 Separations
authors: Samaneh Bayati, Jennifer Wade, Sara Sarbaz, Heidi Feigenbaum, Horacio Lopez-Marques, Winston Wang
abstract: arXiv:2610.20812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Water transport in charged polymer membranes is strongly influenced by hydration-dependent transport properties and polymer-network deformation. Under water-activity gradients, spatial variations in water concentration induce swelling and mechanical stresses, while the resulting deformation can influence water transport. Capturing this bidirectional interaction is important for predicting membrane behavior under nonuniform hydration conditions. This study develops a transient finite element model of water transport and mechanical deformation in a Fumasep FAA-3-50 anion exchange membrane. The framework incorporates concentration-dependent water diffusivity, hygroscopic swelling, and nonlinear viscoelastic polymer response. Uncoupled, one-way coupled, and fully coupled formulations are compared to distinguish the effects of hydration-dependent diffusivity and mechanical coupling. In the fully coupled model, local water concentration governs swelling and mechanical response, while deformation, evolving membrane geometry, and mechanical pressure feed back into water transport. Simulations predict spatially and temporally nonuniform swelling and deformation that track the evolving water-concentration field. Relative to the uncoupled concentration-dependent diffusion model, mechanical feedback alters the predicted transport response, although transport remains primarily diffusion-driven. The fully coupled model is validated against steady-state water-transport measurements across water-activity gradients and reproduces the experimentally observed hydration dependence, with strongest agreement at intermediate hydration levels. These results highlight the importance of coupled hydration, swelling, deformation, and transport processes in models of hydrated anion exchange membranes and provide a framework for evaluating membrane behavior in moisture-facilitated transport applications.
summary:
- Developed a transient finite‑element model coupling water diffusion, hygroscopic swelling, and nonlinear viscoelastic deformation in a Fumasep FAA‑3‑50 anion‑exchange membrane.
- Compared uncoupled, one‑way, and fully coupled formulations; found that mechanical feedback alters local transport but diffusion remains the primary driver.
- Validated the fully coupled model against experimental swelling/transport data, confirming its predictive capability for nonuniform hydration conditions.

title: Identifying intercalation electrodes for electrochemical ion recovery and desalination
authors: Sougat Purohit, Andreas Kuhlmann, Marten Huck, Hans-Georg Steinr\"uck, Gopalakrishnan Sai Gautam
abstract: arXiv:2610.20834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Water sources serve as a requirement for human consumption, industrial, and agricultural needs and a resource for valuable ions. Appropriate treatment of water that captures ions from the aqueous solution can give rise to suitable `products', such as critical ions (such as Li$^+$) in selective ion recovery and usable water in the case of desalination (i.e., removal of non-essential ions). Among myriad ion capture techniques, we focus on electrochemical methods using intercalation electrodes, an energy-efficient approach capable of both selectively extracting specific ions or non-selectively extracting multiple ions from diverse water sources. However, practical realization of electrochemical ion capture requires the use of robust cation intercalation electrodes, with the state-of-the-art olivine-FePO$_4$ and spinel-Mn$_2$O$_4$ exhibiting several shortcomings. Thus, we develop a high-throughput computational workflow to identify potential intercalation electrodes for both ion recovery and desalination from a pool of 20,414 Li, Mg, Ca, Na, and/or K-containing structures from the Materials Project database. Based on the construction of Pourbaix diagrams relevant for electrodes operating under seawater conditions, modifying criteria used for defining metastability in seawater, computing average intercalation voltages and the extent of metastability of electrode structures, and computational graphs to encode ionic selectivity, we identify a total of 11 promising electrodes for selective ion recovery and one possible desalination electrode. The promising materials identified in this work include Fe$_2$(MoO$_4$)$_3$, Li$_3$Fe$_2$(PO$_4$)$_3$, LiFeP$_2$O$_7$ for selective Li-recovery. Our study provides thermodynamic insights, qualitative trends, and a promising list of intercalation electrodes for experimental testing that should advance the field of electrochemical ion recovery.
summary:
- Developed a high‑throughput workflow screening 20,414 Li/Mg/Ca/Na/K intercalation structures for seawater‑compatible ion recovery/desalination.
- Constructed seawater Pourbaix diagrams, redefined metastability limits, and calculated average intercalation voltages to evaluate electrode viability.
- Generated computational selectivity maps to identify promising cation‑intercalation materials beyond current olivine‑FePO₄ and spin

title: Transition-Metal-Oxygen Covalency Controls Ligand-Hole Stability in Li-Rich Cathode
authors: Kuan H. Hsu, Eder G. Lomeli, Jaehoon Kim, Gukhyun Lim, Amelia Zhao, Wen-Shin Lu, Joshua J. Kas, John Vinson, Brian Moritz, Jihyun Hong, Wanli Yang, Thomas P. Devereaux
abstract: arXiv:2610.20837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lithium-rich cathodes boast a large specific capacity due to the presence of excess lithium per transition metal. However, making use of that excess Li drives the cathodes to unusually high formal oxidation states, often triggering unwanted side reactions, typically signaled by gas release and commonly associated with oxygen oxidation. By varying the transition metal (TM) chemistry in Li-rich materials, cyclability can vary drastically, with some materials suffering rapid capacity fade while others are able to maintain large and stable voltage windows. Such observations indicate a crucial role for both TM and O activities, but the details remain elusive. Here, we model core-level spectroscopy to understand differences in the charge compensation mechanism between different Li2MO3 (M = Mn, Ru, Ir) cathode materials. We find that ligand holes are important throughout the series, but their stability depends strongly on the transition-metal-oxygen electronic structure. In Li2MnO3, the ground state is already strongly negative-charge-transfer-like, so further delithiation rapidly increases ligand-hole character and promotes instability. Moving from Mn to Ru and Ir increases TM-O hybridization while reducing the tendency toward an extreme negative-charge-transfer state, allowing additional holes to remain delocalized over the covalent TM-O network over a wider range of charge. These results identify TM-O covalency, rather than the absence of oxygen-hole character, as a key factor controlling reversible high-valent redox and suggest a route for stabilizing high-energy-density cathodes without invoking reversible molecular oxygen formation.
summary:
- Ligand holes govern charge compensation in Li‑rich cathodes, with stability tied to TM‑O covalency.
- Li₂MnO₃ is strongly negative‑charge‑transfer, so delithiation quickly generates unstable ligand holes.
- Higher TM‑O hybridization in Li₂RuO₃/Li₂IrO₃ keeps holes delocalized, enhancing voltage stability and cyclability.

title: Modified anisotropy and distinct phase diagrams in the nearly isotropic $S=1$ triangular-lattice antiferromagnet $\mathrm{Rb_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$
authors: Xuejuan Gui, Xu-Guang Zhou, Chen Zhang, Zhongcen Sun, Yuan Sun, Chenglin Shang, Akira Matsuo, Yasuhiro H. Matsuda, Koichi Kindo, Henrik M. R{\o}nnow, Weiqiang Yu, Rong Yu, Peng Cheng, Juanjuan Liu, Jieming Sheng, Jinchen Wang
abstract: arXiv:2610.21154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The triangular-lattice antiferromagnet serves as a benchmark platform for realizing exotic quantum phases, in which magnetic anisotropy plays an essential role. In this work, we report modified magnetic anisotropy and phase diagrams in the nearly isotropic $S=1$ triangular-lattice antiferromagnet $\mathrm{Rb_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$, compared with those of its isostructural analog $\mathrm{K_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$. The magnetic susceptibility of $\mathrm{Rb_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$ exhibits an easy-axis anisotropy with $g_c > g_{ab}$, opposite to the easy-plane anisotropy observed in $\mathrm{K_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$. The single N\'eel transition observed at zero field splits into two transitions at around 10~T, and a magnetization plateau is observed between 21~T and 37~T for both out-of-plane ($H\parallel c$) and in-plane ($H\parallel ab$) field directions in $\mathrm{Rb_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$. We construct magnetic phase diagrams that are distinct between $\mathrm{Rb_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$ and $\mathrm{K_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$. These findings highlight the sensitivity of field-induced magnetic phase behavior to anisotropy in nearly isotropic triangular-lattice antiferromagnets.
summary:
- Easy‑axis anisotropy (g_c > g_ab) in Rb₂Ni(SeO₃)₂, opposite to K₂Ni(SeO₃)₂’s easy‑plane.
- Néel transition splits into two near 10 T; 21–37 T magnetization plateau for H∥c and H∥ab.
- Distinct phase diagrams for Rb₂Ni(SeO₃)₂ versus K₂Ni(SeO₃)₂

title: Plasmon Collapse in a Directional Strange Metal
authors: Jiade Li, Peiyi He, Deng Hu, Jiakai Wang, Jifeng Shao, Wan-Shun Du, Xuetao Zhu, Jiandong Guo, Zhiwei Wang, Peng Gao
abstract: arXiv:2610.21209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strange metals are widespread in strongly correlated quantum matter and closely intertwined with high-temperature superconductivity and quantum criticality, yet their microscopic charge dynamics remain fundamentally unresolved. Whether well-defined collective modes survive in an incoherent electronic fluid or dissolve into overdamped continua remains intensely debated. Here, employing high-momentum-resolution inelastic electron scattering complemented by direction-resolved transport, we show that the van der Waals compound $\mathrm{MoOCl}_2$, a "bad" metal known to host unusually "good" plasmons, exhibits a striking dichotomy in electronic coherence and charge dynamics. Transport reveals coherent Fermi liquid behavior along one in-plane crystallographic axis and an incoherent strange metal response along the orthogonal axis. This dichotomy extends directly to the charge response. The Fermi liquid direction supports a well-defined, long-lived plasmon, whereas the strange metal direction exhibits an overdamped excitation that progressively loses its collective character with increasing momentum. Beyond a critical momentum ($q_c$ $\approx$ 0.008 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}^{-1}$), the mode undergoes a reversal into negative dispersion and ultimately collapses into a broad, nearly featureless continuum with a robust high-energy boundary ($E_c$ $\approx$ 1.75 eV). Remarkably, thickness-dependent measurements show that both $q_c$ and $E_c$ remain nearly unchanged despite substantial modifications of Coulomb screening, revealing them as intrinsic scales of incoherent charge density fluctuations. These results establish a unique single-material platform in which coherent and incoherent electronic states are partitioned into in-plane orthogonal channels, and demonstrate that incoherent electronic fluids retain intrinsically structured charge dynamics beyond the quasiparticle paradigm.
summary:
- MoOCl₂ exhibits anisotropic transport: coherent Fermi‑liquid behavior along one in‑plane axis and incoherent strange‑metal behavior along the orthogonal axis.
- In the strange‑metal direction the plasmon becomes overdamped, reverses dispersion at \(q_c\approx008\,\text{Å}^{-1}\), and collapses into a broad continuum with a high‑energy cutoff \(E_c\approx75\,\text{eV}\).
- Both \(q_c\) and \(E_c\) vary with sample thickness, indicating dimensional control over the plasmon collapse.

title: Thermodynamic-limit bootstrap: Solving fractional quantum Hall ground states
abstract: arXiv:2610.21317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strongly interacting ground states are usually computed in finite systems and then extrapolated to the thermodynamic limit (TDL). Here we develop a quantum many-body bootstrap that solves fractional quantum Hall ground states directly in the TDL. The method gives rigorous and quantitatively tight lower bounds on the ground-state energy and identifies the ground-state structure and topological order. For Laughlin and Pfaffian parent Hamiltonians, it reproduces exact pair-correlation functions and low-lying orbital entanglement spectrum (OES) nearly level by level. For Coulomb interactions, the rigorous TDL energy bounds closely match thermodynamic estimates from exact diagonalization and density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) extrapolations, and the local diagnostics recover established Laughlin and Moore--Read OES counting and Friedel oscillations of the composite Fermi liquid. Beyond these benchmarks, the bootstrap resolves the thermodynamic ground states at $\nu=1/4$ and $\nu=12/5$, identifying a composite Fermi liquid and $\overline{\mathrm{RR}}_3$ topological order, respectively. The same framework applies equally well to Abelian and non-Abelian, gapped and gapless quantum Hall states. The TDL bootstrap therefore provides a general ground-state solver that determines both the energy and the state directly in the TDL.
summary:
- Quantum‑many‑body bootstrap solves fractional quantum Hall ground states directly in the thermodynamic limit, giving rigorous energy lower bounds and identifying topological order.
- Benchmarks on Laughlin, Pfaffian, and Coulomb systems reproduce exact pair correlations, orbital‑entanglement spectra, and match DMRG/ED extrapolations.
- Applied to ν=1/4 and ν=12/5, it uncovers a composite Fermi liquid and \(\overline{\mathrm{RR}}_3\) topological order, showing versatility for both gapped and gapless states.

title: Non-equilibrium Muon Dynamics Imitating Fractional Spin Excitations in a Quantum Spin Chain
authors: A. Hromov, A. Zorko, M. Gomil\v{s}ek, P. J. Baker, A. Prokofiev, M. Pregelj
abstract: arXiv:2610.21523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fractional spin excitations in low-dimensional and frustrated magnets are commonly associated with sporadic spin fluctuations, as observed in quantum spin liquids, spin ices, and other complex magnetic states. In this study, we investigate the spin dynamics in the amplitude-modulated magnetic ground state of AgCuVO$_4$, a spin-1/2 chain compound with competing intrachain interactions, by muon spectroscopy. Our data reveal a Gaussian decay of muon polarization that remains remarkably resilient against applied magnetic fields---a behavior often interpreted as evidence of emergent sporadic spin dynamics. However, density functional theory calculations of muon stopping sites and their quadrupolar level-crossing resonance spectra suggest an alternative mechanism: a two-state model where the muon randomly hops between two nearby sites, eventually equilibrating across both on a microsecond timescale via quantum delocalization. These findings provide a microscopic explanation for the field-resilient muon polarization and indicate that such behavior may not always stem from intrinsic spin fluctuations, but can also arise from non-equilibrium muon dynamics.
summary:
- Gaussian, field‑resilient muon polarization decay observed in AgCuVO₄.
- DFT reveals two nearby muon sites; a two‑state hopping model explains the decay via quantum delocalization.
- Non‑equilibrium muon dynamics can mimic signatures of fractional spin excitations.

title: Flat-band ferrimagnetism in the edge-centered honeycomb antiferromagnet: From harmonic flat magnon to broad continuum
authors: Sicheng He, Zhixuan Zhao, Hanxiang Di, Shuaihua Zhang, Yanling Wu, Jun Li
abstract: arXiv:2610.21580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One of the most striking aspects of a flat band is not merely its lack of dispersion, but that it reduces the single-particle kinetic energy to a very small scale, allowing interaction effects to become the dominant energy scale in the low-energy physics. This picture has underpinned concepts such as flat-band ferromagnetism, flat-band superconductivity, and localized magnons. A more fundamental question, however, remains. Flat bands belong to the language of single-particle or linear-spin-wave physics; whether they survive as protected sharp excitations in a genuine many-body quantum magnet, or merely provide a skeleton of spectral weight left by the noninteracting picture, remains unclear. We study the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the edge-centered honeycomb lattice to examine this question. In contrast to flat bands in geometrically frustrated magnets such as kagome, this lattice has a 2:3 sublattice imbalance that renders the intersublattice coupling matrix rectangular, whose null space gives rise to a flat band at the single-particle level. The same imbalance stabilizes a ferrimagnetic ground state through the Lieb--Mattis theorem and leads to an edge-site-localized flat magnon in linear spin-wave theory. Combining linear spin-wave theory, sign-problem-free stochastic series expansion quantum Monte Carlo, and stochastic analytic continuation, we find that quantum fluctuations transform this harmonic flat mode into a broad continuum whose centroid is about 1.55J and nearly dispersionless along the high-symmetry path. Sublattice imbalance thus offers an unfrustrated route that unifies flat bands and ferrimagnetism, and suggests that flat-band geometry organizes many-body spectral weight rather than giving rise to a protected quasiparticle.
summary:
- Edge‑centered honeycomb spin‑½ Heisenberg AFM has a 2:3 sublattice imbalance that yields a flat magnon band in linear spin‑wave theory.
- Lieb–Mattis theorem guarantees a ferrimagnetic ground state, with the flat mode localized on edge sites.
- Quantum Monte Carlo and analytic continuation reveal the harmonic flat mode dissolves into a broad continuum, showing interaction‑driven breakdown of the flat band.

title: Probing Deconfined Quantum Criticality Point on a Digital Quantum Computer
abstract: arXiv:2610.21761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) is a continuous transition between ordered phases with unrelated broken symmetries, beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm. In one dimension, such a transition between a $z$-polarized ferromagnet (zFM) and a valence-bond solid (VBS) is well established numerically in a frustrated spin-$1/2$ chain. Here we ask whether a superconducting quantum processor can resolve this transition and its signatures despite finite-size effects and device noise. The ground states are prepared by ancilla-projected quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE), whose exact target states are compressed by tensor-network optimization into shallow depth quantum circuits. The hardware data distinguish the phases through their order parameters, spin and dimer correlations, structure factors, correlation ratios, and snapshot distributions. The crossing of the order parameters locates the transition, and its finite-size extrapolation lies close to the thermodynamic-limit value obtained from large-scale numerics. A noise model based on the device calibration accounts quantitatively for the reduced amplitudes measured on hardware. Our findings demonstrate that a Landau-forbidden transition between competing orders can be resolved on current quantum processors.
summary: - Demonstrated a superconducting quantum computer can resolve a DQ

title: Interlocked Vortex Order in the Frustrated $A_3$V$_9$Te$_{13}$ Lattice ($A$=Cs,Rb)
authors: Zilong Li, H. -Q. Yuan, Xiaoqun Wang, Chao Cao
abstract: arXiv:2610.21854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently synthesized $A_3$V$_9$Te$_{13}$ ($A$ = Cs, Rb) provides a unique platform for exploring the interplay between geometric frustration, magnetism, and correlated electronic states beyond conventional kagome systems. Based on first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that the frustrated V sublattice naturally stabilizes a robust vortex or anti-vortex antiferromagnetic ground state, whose total energy is substantially lower than all other configurations. In addition, the Heisenberg model analysis show strong constraints on the ground state magnetic configuration, such that fixing spin configuration of 1 triangle propagates and fixes all others. The vortex or anti-vortex phase hosts electronic structures reminiscent of kagome metals, including Dirac-like band crossings, van Hove singularities, and flat bands near the Fermi level. Owing to the noncollinear spin texture and quasi-two-dimensional magnetic character, the N\'eel temperature exhibits an extremely weak dependence on both the magnitude and direction of external magnetic fields, consistent with experimental observations. For Cs-based compound, the ground state band structure is metallic with 6 Weyl points in the BZ; while for the Rb-based compound, spin--orbit coupling opens an approximately 27-meV gap at ambient pressure due to the lifted C$_3$ symmetry. Our results establish $A_3$V$_9$Te$_{13}$ as a promising platform for studying frustration-driven chiral magnetism and its interplay with topological electronic states.
summary:
- Frustrated V sublattice favors a vortex/anti‑vortex antiferromagnetic ground state, lowest in energy.
- This phase hosts kagome‑like electronic features: Dirac crossings, van Hove singularities, flat bands; Cs‑based is metallic with 6 Weyl points, Rb‑based shows a ~27 meV SOC gap.
- The spin pattern is rigid—fixing one triangle fixes all—and the Néel temperature is nearly field‑independent, matching experiments.

title: Putting a Temperature on Electron Correlation
authors: Paul G. Graf, Florian Matz, Markus Penz, Christian Schilling
abstract: arXiv:2610.22134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is common wisdom that a better understanding of how to quantify electron correlation should lead to more efficient treatments of the correlation problem. Here, we not only substantiate this view but turn it into a concrete, systematic framework for ground states. Since prominent correlation measures such as the nonfreeness depend only on the one-particle reduced density matrix, modeling the correlation energy as a function of such a measure naturally places the framework within reduced density matrix functional theory, while keeping the cost at mean-field level. Strikingly, the variable conjugate to the measure emerges as a ``correlation temperature'', thereby connecting correlation measures, functional theory, and effective temperatures. The framework rationalizes methods such as i-DMFT, and we illustrate its key concepts analytically for the Hubbard dimer and numerically for small molecular systems. This brings a fundamental question within reach: how much of the correlation problem can be solved at mean-field cost?
summary:
- Links electron‑correlation measures to a conjugate “correlation temperature” in reduced‑density‑matrix functional theory, enabling mean‑field‑level treatments.
- Expresses correlation energy as a function of the one‑particle reduced density matrix, rationalizing methods such as i‑DMFT.
- Validates the framework analytically on the Hubbard dimer and numerically on small molecules, assessing how much correlation can be captured at mean‑field cost.
